strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1.06M samples) is 6-10× larger than prior MER datasets with balanced length distribution and diverse expression types (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE), addressing important gaps in real-world MER benchmarking

Comprehensive evaluation methodology: Four-way test categorization (simple/complex printed, screen-captured, handwritten) provides nuanced assessment and clearly reveals existing methods' failures on complex/noisy expressions

Strong and consistent empirical results: Outperforms SOTA across all test categories with significant improvements on complex expressions (+0.226 BLEU over Pix2tex on CPE) and competitive results on handwritten benchmarks
Systematic ablation studies: Tables 2-4 effectively isolate contributions of dataset diversity, data augmentation, and LAM components
Practical value: Addresses important real-world MER challenges (length variation, noise, domain diversity) with working system and dataset release
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Core contribution is standard Swin Transformer + mBART encoder-decoder; Length-Aware Module (LAM) is relatively simple (attention + pooling + MLP), with marginal empirical benefit (Table 4: ~2% BLEU on CPE, <1% on most other sets), raising questions about necessity and complexity-benefit tradeoff

Unfair comparison with prior methods: Comparing UniMERNet (trained on 1.06M samples) against Pix2tex (158K) and Texify (30K) conflates dataset scale with architectural improvements; critical missing ablation is retraining Pix2tex/Texify on UniMER-1M to isolate model contributions from data scale effects

Insufficient dataset novelty: SPE/CPE are purely synthetic (rendered LaTeX); SCE contains only ~4,744 unique samples from PDFs; HWE is straightforward combination of existing CROHME + HME100K datasets; missing details on data balancing strategy, inter-annotator agreement, and automatic annotation error rates

Incomplete experimental analysis: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; missing computational cost analysis (inference speed, model size, memory); lacks error analysis, failure mode characterization, and explanation of when/why LAM helps; ExpRate metric inconsistently reported

Orthogonal augmentation benefits: Image augmentation improvements (Table 3) are independent of architectural design and could benefit any baseline model, making it difficult to isolate UniMERNet's specific contributions

Limited scope of 'real-world': Only evaluates LaTeX output; SCE sampling from 1,000 PDFs may not fully represent document diversity; no end-to-end document understanding evaluation; claims of 'universal' and 'unprecedented' are somewhat overstated

Methodological details underspecified: 'Length' definition unclear (tokens vs. characters); SmoothL1 loss choice for length prediction not justified; loss weight selection (λ₁=1, λ₂=0.5) arbitrary without ablation; LAM architectural modifications to mBART not precisely detailed
Minimal qualitative analysis: Figure 5 shows only 3 examples; no systematic error analysis or discussion of limitations; insufficient examination of when and why the proposed method fails

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1.06M samples) represents a significant advance in scale and diversity over prior MER datasets (100k-200k), with thoughtful coverage of multiple formula types (SPE, CPE, SCE, HWE) and real-world scenarios

Comprehensive evaluation benchmark: UniMER-Test with 23,789 diverse samples addresses documented gaps in existing benchmarks, particularly for complex, noisy, and handwritten expressions, establishing a valuable new evaluation standard

Thorough experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies, depth configuration analysis, augmentation impact assessment, and pre-training analysis provide solid empirical support with multiple metrics (BLEU, EditDistance, ExpRate)

Well-motivated architecture: The three identified challenges (visual similarity, spatial information, inference speed) are clearly articulated and the proposed solutions (FGE, CE, RSW, SA) follow logically from these constraints

Reproducibility focus: Detailed implementation specifications (hyperparameters, rendering settings, augmentation procedures, XeLaTeX configuration) and commitment to release code/data support reproducibility
Practical efficiency gains: Achieves ~23% speed improvement (5.06 vs. 4.12 FPS) while maintaining or improving accuracy, valuable for real-world deployment
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Individual components (FGE: modified patch embedding; CE: standard depthwise convolution; SA: ResNet's squeeze-excitation) are established techniques. The paper presents engineering optimization rather than algorithmic innovation

Data-model attribution ambiguity: Table 5 reveals that when Texify is trained on UniMER-1M, residual improvements over UniMERNet are modest (SPE: +0.009, CPE: +0.025, SCE: +0.027 BLEU). Most performance gains stem from the dataset rather than architectural contributions

Data contamination risk not adequately addressed: 89% of UniMER-1M LaTeX comes from ArXiv; Table 6 shows 16M additional image-text pairs from ArXiv used for pre-training. The paper does not credibly rule out formula overlap between training/pre-training and test sets, and SPE explicitly reuses Pix2tex's test set

Insufficient statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or bootstrap analysis. Performance differences of 1-2% on smaller subsets (HWE: 6,332 samples) lack statistical justification. No inter-annotator agreement reported for manual SCE annotation

Incomplete real-world performance analysis: Despite the title's claim of 'real-world' capability, absolute performance on realistic data remains limited (SCE: 0.626 BLEU; HWE improvement +0.007 BLEU vs. Texify*). HWE gains minimal benefit from ArXiv-heavy pre-training, yet this limitation is underexplored

Pre-training data inaccessibility and underspecification: The 16M image-text pairs are described as 'in-house' and unavailable, compromising reproducibility. The procedure for creating pre-training data lacks documentation, making results difficult for others to verify or extend

Overstated claims about universality: Title and framing claim 'universal' and 'real-world' capabilities, but performance gaps on authentic data (SCE, HWE) and small absolute gains on handwritten expressions contradict these claims

Absence of systematic error analysis: Only 3 cherry-picked qualitative examples in Figure 5. No investigation of failure modes, performance by formula complexity/length, or systematic categorization of errors

Missing reproduction details: LaTeX normalization rules stated as 'adjusted' but not formally specified; Squeeze Attention's dimensionality reduction factor not quantified; perceptual hashing threshold for SCE deduplication not provided
